stem: Which energy transfer takes place in an electric motor?

options.content: Electrical energy to kinetic energy
Kinetic energy to electrical energy
Chemical energy to electrical energy
Thermal energy to kinetic energy

explanation: A motor transfers electrical energy into kinetic energy (with some thermal energy wasted).

stem: Which change does NOT increase the turning effect on the coil of a d.c. motor?

options.content: Reversing the current
options.rationale: Correct: this reverses the rotation instead.

options.content: Adding more turns to the coil
Increasing the current
Using a stronger magnet

explanation: More turns, more current and a stronger field increase the turning effect; reversing the current only reverses the direction.

stem: What is the job of the split-ring commutator in a d.c. motor?

options.content: To change the a.c. supply into d.c. for the coil
To increase the current in the coil as it turns faster
options.rationale: It only switches the current's direction.

options.content: To reverse the coil current each half turn so it keeps turning
To hold the curved magnets in place around the turning coil
options.rationale: The commutator is on the axle, not on the magnets.

explanation: The commutator reverses the coil current every half turn, keeping the turning effect in the same direction.

stem: What are the brushes in a d.c. motor?

options.content: Parts that sweep dust out of the motor as it spins
options.rationale: They carry current, despite the name.

options.content: Contacts pressing on the commutator to carry current to the coil
The permanent magnets that provide the field
options.rationale: The field comes from the magnets, not the brushes.

options.content: The steel axle on which the coil turns
options.rationale: The axle supports the coil; brushes carry current.

explanation: Springy carbon brushes keep electrical contact with the spinning commutator.

stem: The turning effect on a motor coil is largest when the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field.
explanation: Then the forces on the sides act furthest from the axle; when the coil is at right angles to the field the turning effect is zero.

stem: A rectangular coil is placed in a magnetic field and connected straight to a battery, with no commutator. What happens when the current is switched on?

options.content: It spins continuously in the same direction, like a motor.
options.rationale: Without a commutator the forces stop helping after half a turn.

options.content: It does not move at all, as the two forces cancel out.
options.rationale: It turns until it reaches the vertical position.

options.content: It turns until its plane is at 90° to the field, then stops.
It spins faster and faster until it burns out.
options.rationale: Without a commutator it cannot keep turning.

explanation: Without a commutator the current never reverses, so after the coil passes the vertical the forces turn it back: it settles at right angles to the field.
hints: What do the forces on the sides do once the coil has passed the vertical position?

stem: In a d.c. motor, there is no turning effect when the coil is vertical. Why does the coil not stop there?

options.content: The brushes give it a small push round at that point.
Momentum carries it past, and the reversed current turns it on.
Gravity pulls the heavier side of the coil round.
options.rationale: The coil is balanced; gravity does not turn it.

options.content: The commutator stores energy and releases it there.
options.rationale: A commutator only switches the current.

explanation: The coil's momentum carries it through the vertical position; the commutator has reversed the current, so the forces keep turning it the same way.
hints: What keeps a moving object moving when no force acts?

stem: A d.c. motor turns clockwise. The connections to the battery are swapped. What happens?

options.content: It turns clockwise, faster.
It stops.
It turns clockwise, slower.
It turns anticlockwise.

explanation: Reversing the current reverses the forces on the coil, so the motor turns the other way.

stem: Why do the two long sides of a motor coil experience forces in opposite directions?

options.content: The magnetic field points in opposite directions at the two sides.
options.rationale: The field between the poles is in one direction.

options.content: One side is made of a different metal.
Only one side is in the field.
options.rationale: Both sides are in the field.

options.content: The current flows in opposite directions in the two sides.

explanation: The current goes along one side and back along the other, so by the left-hand rule the forces are opposite.

stem: Match each part of a d.c. motor with its job.

right.content: Carries the current that feels the forces
Reverses the current in the coil every half turn
Carry the current to the rotating commutator

explanation: Commutator: reversing. Brushes: contact. Magnets: field. Coil: current-carrying conductor.

stem: Select **all** the changes that would make a d.c. motor spin faster.

options.content: Removing the commutator
options.rationale: The motor would stop turning continuously.

options.content: Reversing the magnets
Adding more turns to the coil
Increasing the current
Swapping the battery connections
Using stronger magnets

explanation: A larger turning effect (more current, more turns, stronger field) makes the motor spin faster.
hints: Which changes increase the size of the forces on the coil?

stem: Name the part of a d.c. motor that reverses the current in the coil every half turn.
explanation: The split-ring commutator reverses the current in the coil every half turn.

stem: A simple d.c. motor has a rectangular coil between the poles of two magnets. The coil is connected to a battery through a split-ring commutator and brushes.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain why the coil starts to turn when the current is switched on.

points.description: The current flows in opposite directions in the two sides of the coil, which are in the magnetic field
so (by Fleming's left-hand rule) one side is pushed up and the other down, giving a turning effect

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why the coil keeps turning in the same direction.

points.description: Every half turn, as the coil passes the vertical, the commutator reverses the current in the coil
so the force on each side reverses as it moves to the other pole, keeping the turning effect in the same direction

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: How could the motor be made to turn the other way?

options.content: Add more turns to the coil
Use a larger current
Use stronger magnets
Reverse the battery connections

parts.explanation: Reversing the current (or the field) reverses the rotation.

explanation: Opposite currents in the two sides give opposite forces and a turning effect; the commutator keeps it turning one way.
hints: Use Fleming's left-hand rule on each side of the coil.
